title: Why some volcanoes explode
teaches: How the silica and water in magma decide whether a volcano pours out lava or explodes, and what a pyroclastic flow is

blocks.text: In 1902 Saint-Pierre was the largest town on Martinique, in the French Caribbean: a port of about 28,000 people, with a theatre, a cathedral and ships from Europe in its harbour. Seven kilometres to the north rose Mont Pelée, a volcano that had last erupted, mildly, in 1851. In late April 1902 it began to throw out ash, and the smell of sulphur hung over the town. On 5 May a torrent of mud and boulders rushed down a valley and buried a sugar works on the coast, killing about 150 people. The governor appointed a commission, which reported that the town was in no immediate danger, and most people stayed.

At about eight o'clock on the morning of 8 May, a black cloud burst from the side of the mountain and rolled down towards the town. It reached the harbour in about a minute. Within a few minutes almost everyone in Saint-Pierre was dead, along with most of the crews of the ships at anchor. Only two people in the town are known for certain to have survived: Ludger Sylbaris, a prisoner shut in a thick-walled cell, and Léon Compère-Léandre, a shoemaker on the edge of town. Both were badly burned. No lava had flowed anywhere near the town. Whatever killed it had travelled faster than any lava flow, and was gone in minutes.

blocks.caption: The ruins of Saint-Pierre after 8 May 1902, with Mont Pelée behind.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: On 8 May 1902 Mont Pelée on Martinique destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre, 7 km away, killing about 28,000 people in minutes.
No lava flow reached the town; something else came down the mountain, far faster than lava.

blocks.text: The French Academy of Sciences sent the mineralogist Alfred Lacroix to find out what had happened. He arrived in June and stayed for months, watching the volcano from observation posts around it. Pelée had not finished. A dome of stiff lava was swelling in its crater, too thick to flow away, and from its broken sides, again and again, more of the black clouds burst out and swept down the slopes.

Lacroix watched them closely. Each one was a dense, churning avalanche of hot ash, rock fragments and gas. It did not rise into the sky like smoke; it poured downhill, hugging the ground and following the valleys, at speeds he estimated at well over 100 kilometres an hour. It flowed because it was heavier than air, a fluid made of solid fragments held apart by hot gas. In Saint-Pierre the walls had been knocked down in the direction the cloud travelled, wood had been charred, and glass had softened. Lacroix called it a *nuée ardente*, a glowing cloud. Today it is called a **pyroclastic flow** (from the Greek for fire and broken), and it is the deadliest thing a volcano does.

Lacroix's 1904 book about the eruption described the dome, the glowing clouds and the volcano's later habits so carefully that eruptions of Pelée's kind are still called Peléan. His question, though, went deeper than Martinique. Kilauea in Hawaii had been famous for decades for its lake of molten lava, which visitors walked up to and watched. Why did one volcano pour out its magma, while another blew its magma apart?

blocks.caption: Alfred Lacroix (1863–1948), who studied Mont Pelée's eruption from 1902 to 1903 and named the nuée ardente.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Alfred Lacroix watched Pelée's later eruptions and described the nuée ardente, now called a pyroclastic flow.
A pyroclastic flow is a ground-hugging avalanche of hot ash, rock and gas, heavier than air, that can travel at over 100 km/h.
At Pelée the flows broke from a dome of stiff lava swelling in the crater.

blocks.text: The answer lies in two things: the gas dissolved in the magma, and how sticky the magma is. Deep underground, **magma** (molten rock still below ground; once it pours out on the surface it is called lava) holds water and a smaller amount of carbon dioxide dissolved in it, a few per cent by weight, kept there by the pressure of the rock above. A bottle of soda works the same way. While the cap is on, the gas stays dissolved and you cannot see it; open the bottle, the pressure drops, and bubbles appear. As magma rises towards the surface, the pressure on it falls, and the water comes out of solution as bubbles of steam. The bubbles grow as they rise, because the pressure keeps dropping, and by the time the magma nears the surface its gas may take up hundreds of times the volume it did at depth.

What happens next depends on how easily the bubbles can move. Lesson 4 showed that silica makes magma sticky: silicon and oxygen atoms link into chains and networks that the melt has to drag past each other to flow. Hawaiian basalt is about 50% silica. At eruption temperature it is about as runny as warm syrup, and bubbles in it can rise, join and escape, so the gas leaves ahead of the magma. Rhyolite, at more than 70% silica, can be a hundred million times stiffer. Bubbles in it cannot escape; they stay where they formed and keep growing, until the magma becomes a foam. When gas fills about three-quarters of the volume, the bubbles are packed so tightly that the thin walls of melt between them can no longer hold, and the foam tears apart into shreds of melt and expanding gas that shoot up the vent. That breaking up, called **fragmentation**, is the explosion, and the shreds cool into **volcanic ash**, which is not burnt material but tiny fragments of glass and crystal.

blocks.caption: A batch of magma rising up an 8 km conduit. As the pressure falls, water comes out as bubbles. The graph shows what share of the magma is gas; the dashed line is where a foam breaks apart.
blocks.task: Erupt Pinatubo's magma, then find a magma that reaches the surface without exploding

blocks.text: Both ingredients matter. Sticky magma that has lost most of its gas, as Pelée's dome had, does not explode as it reaches the surface; it oozes out and piles up as a dome. A dome, though, is a dangerous thing. It sits steep and unstable over a vent full of gas-rich magma, and when part of it collapses, the weight that was holding in the gas-rich magma beneath is suddenly gone. Like a shaken bottle uncapped, that magma froths and fragments at once. That is how Pelée's glowing clouds broke from its sides. Runny magma rich in gas, on the other hand, produces fountains of lava hundreds of metres high, as on Kilauea, but the gas still has a way out and the fountains do not shatter into an explosion.

blocks.caption: A lava fountain at Kilauea, Hawaii. Gas escapes easily from runny basalt, throwing up molten lava rather than blasting it into ash.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Magma holds water dissolved under pressure; as it rises, the water comes out as bubbles that grow as the pressure falls.
In runny, low-silica magma such as Hawaiian basalt, bubbles rise and escape, so the eruption is gentle.
In sticky, high-silica magma the bubbles are trapped; when gas fills about three-quarters of the volume, the foam fragments into ash and gas: an explosion.
Sticky magma that has lost its gas piles up as a lava dome, which can collapse and trigger explosions and pyroclastic flows.

blocks.text: Once the magma has fragmented, the mixture of gas and ash leaves the vent at hundreds of metres a second. At first it is much denser than air, a jet thrown upward by its own speed. As it rises it draws air in at its edges, and the hot ash heats that air, which expands. If enough air is pulled in before the jet slows down, the whole mixture becomes lighter than the surrounding air and keeps rising on its own, like a hot-air balloon, as a **plume** that can reach 20 to 40 kilometres high before spreading out sideways into an umbrella. If not, the jet runs out of speed while still heavier than air, falls back around the vent, and pours down the mountain as a pyroclastic flow.

blocks.caption: An eruption jet leaving a vent. Whether it rises as a plume or collapses depends on how fast it leaves (set by the gas in the magma) and how much ash pours out each second (set by the width of the vent).

blocks.text: Both happened at Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines in June 1991. Scientists from the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology and the US Geological Survey had watched the volcano's earthquakes and gas for two months and warned of an eruption, and tens of thousands of people were evacuated, including those at the US Clark Air Base nearby. On 15 June the climactic eruption sent a plume about 35 kilometres high, while parts of the column collapsed and pyroclastic flows filled valleys around the mountain with ash up to 200 metres deep. The eruption threw out about five cubic kilometres of magma, roughly ten times as much as Mount St Helens in 1980, and its sulphur gas cooled the whole Earth by about half a degree Celsius for the next year. Because of the warnings, the death toll was in the hundreds rather than the tens of thousands.

blocks.caption: Mount Pinatubo's eruption column on 12 June 1991, three days before the largest blast.

blocks.text: Geologists rank eruptions on the **Volcanic Explosivity Index**,[^vei] from 0 for gentle Hawaiian lava flows to 8 for the largest eruptions known. Pinatubo was a 6. The same volcanic arcs that line subduction zones (lesson 11) produce most explosive eruptions, because their magmas are rich in water carried down by the sinking plate, and in silica, which they gain as they melt some of the thick crust they rise through and leave iron- and magnesium-rich crystals behind (lesson 6). The Cascade volcanoes of the Pacific Northwest are among them, and the Cascadia branch of this course follows two of their eruptions.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: An erupting jet of gas and ash rises as a buoyant plume if it draws in and heats enough air before it slows down.
If it slows too soon, still heavier than air, the column collapses and pours down the slopes as pyroclastic flows.
Pinatubo, 1991, did both; warnings and evacuations saved tens of thousands of lives.
Volcanoes above subduction zones produce most explosive eruptions, because their magma is rich in silica and water.

blocks.caption: Six questions on explosive volcanoes
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

choices: A pyroclastic flow: an avalanche of hot ash, rock and gas that raced down the mountain
A lava flow that reached the town over several hours
Ash falling from a high plume that collapsed the roofs over a day
items.why: No lava reached the town. A dense, ground-hugging cloud of hot ash and gas, Lacroix's nuée ardente, crossed the 7 km to the town in about a minute.

items.ask: Why does water come out of magma as bubbles as it rises?
choices: The pressure on it falls, so it can hold less water dissolved
The magma heats up as it nears the surface
Rainwater soaks into the top of the conduit
items.why: Like the gas in a bottle of soda, the water stays dissolved only under pressure. As the pressure drops, it comes out of solution.

items.ask: Two magmas hold the same amount of water. One is basalt with 50% silica, the other rhyolite with 74%. Which is more likely to explode, and why?
choices: The rhyolite, because its stiff melt traps the bubbles until the foam breaks apart
The basalt, because it is hotter
Neither, because explosions depend only on water
items.why: Bubbles rise and escape through runny basalt, but stay trapped in sticky rhyolite and keep growing until the foam fragments.

items.ask: What is volcanic ash made of?
choices: Tiny fragments of volcanic glass and crystals from magma torn apart by expanding gas
Burnt vegetation from the volcano's slopes
items.why: Ash is not the remains of burning. It forms when foamy magma fragments, and the shreds of melt cool instantly into glass.

items.ask: During an eruption the vent widens, so much more ash pours out each second while the gas stays the same. What is likely to happen?
choices: The column can no longer draw in enough air, collapses and sends pyroclastic flows down the slopes
The plume rises higher, because more ash goes up
The eruption stops, because the gas is spread more thinly
items.why: A wider jet needs more speed to mix in enough air to become buoyant. Without it, the column falls back while still heavier than air.

items.ask: Why are most explosive volcanoes found in arcs above subduction zones?
choices: Their magmas are rich in silica and in water carried down by the sinking plate
They are the hottest volcanoes on Earth
Subduction zones have thinner crust for the gas to escape through
items.why: Water released from the sinking slab makes the mantle melt (lesson 11), and the magma that rises through thick crust gains silica. Both make explosions more likely.

summary: **Pelée killed Saint-Pierre without lava.** On 8 May 1902 a pyroclastic flow reached the town in about a minute.
**Pyroclastic flows are hot avalanches of ash and gas.** Heavier than air, they pour down slopes at more than 100 km/h.
**Magma carries dissolved water.** As it rises and the pressure falls, the water comes out as growing bubbles.
**Silica decides whether gas escapes.** Bubbles leave runny basalt but are trapped in sticky rhyolite.
**A foam that is three-quarters gas fragments.** The shreds become ash, and the eruption is explosive.
**Plumes rise if they take in enough air.** Otherwise the column collapses into pyroclastic flows.
**Arc volcanoes are the explosive ones.** Their magmas are rich in silica and water.

vei.title: The Volcanic Explosivity Index
vei.text: Proposed by Chris Newhall and Stephen Self in 1982, the index is based mainly on the volume of material thrown out and the height of the plume. Each step up, from 2 onwards, means about ten times more material. Mount St Helens in 1980 was a 5, Pinatubo in 1991 a 6, Tambora in 1815 a 7. The last 8 was the eruption of Taupō in New Zealand about 26,000 years ago.
